clue.text: Record snub

blocks.note: first meaning: to write down or enter in a register
second meaning: a crushing, dismissive remark

explanation.surface: A record company or chart cold-shoulders someone.
explanation.walkthrough: As a verb phrase, put down means to write down; hyphenated as a noun, a put-down is a snub.
explanation.definitionFit: Entering something in writing is putting it down, and a humiliating dismissive remark is called a put-down.

clue.text: Steal the limelight from the coach to London

blocks.note: travel towards the capital is traditionally going up to London
a stage, short for stagecoach, is a horse-drawn coach

explanation.surface: Someone arriving on the London coach grabs all the attention.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage you go up to London from anywhere else, so 'to London' gives the direction word.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor who moves upstage forces others to turn away from the audience, hence taking attention from fellow performers.

clue.text: The medicine goes down

blocks.note: first meaning: liquid medicine given a little at a time, as for eyes or ears
second meaning: falls or descends

explanation.surface: Mary Poppins territory: the medicine is swallowed.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one sentence about swallowing a dose, but it splits into a noun and a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Eye or ear medicine is administered in small liquid portions, and something that falls or descends is said to do this.

clue.text: Composer crossing street to see lexicographer

indicators.note: the composer is placed across the street, straddling it so the shorter word sits within

blocks.note: Carl Maria von Weber, German composer of Der Freischütz
standard abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A composer crosses the road to visit a dictionary-maker.
explanation.walkthrough: WEBER takes ST into its middle to give WEBSTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Noah Webster compiled the famous American dictionary, so he is the classic example of a dictionary compiler.

clue.text: Moth getting by without extreme poverty

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one word stands on either side of the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the eggar is a family of large brownish moths

explanation.surface: A moth scraping by without much to live on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' here has its old sense of outside, as in the hymn 'a green hill far away, without a city wall'. 'Without extreme' looks like a phrase but splits between indicator and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Beggary is the state of a beggar, which is utter destitution or penury.

clue.text: Supplies the same in every way?

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for the same inside the set of directions

blocks.note: all four compass directions: east, north, west, south
do is short for ditto, meaning the same

explanation.surface: A puzzle about providing things identically in all respects.
explanation.walkthrough: DO, the abbreviation for ditto, sits inside the four points of the compass, E N ... W S; the question mark admits the compass points come in an unusual order.
explanation.definitionFit: To endow is to provide or furnish with something, such as a fund or quality, so it matches supplies as a verb.

clue.text: Adhesive setting for tooth and tongue

blocks.note: teeth are set in the gums
tongue means language, and Arabic is one

explanation.surface: A dentist's glue for fixing a tooth and tongue in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' looks anatomical beside 'tooth', but it means a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Gum arabic is the resin of acacia trees, used as a water-soluble glue on stamps and envelopes.

clue.text: Screen left out round solderer

indicators.note: left stands for its usual abbreviation, and out says to remove it from the word
turned round, the remaining letters are spun into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A workman who solders is left outside, round a screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' is L, which is taken out of SOLDERER; the seven remaining letters are then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A reredos is an ornamental partition or panel behind a church altar, a kind of decorative screen.

clue.text: Group playing north or south lost Elgin marbles, perhaps

indicators.note: a group playing moves about, so these letters are put through their paces in a new order

blocks.note: N and S are the abbreviations for the two compass points, joined by the word or
taken as written

explanation.surface: Greece's lost Elgin Marbles, now in the British Museum, wandering north or south.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition comes twice: the rock band, and a jokey description of marbles, which are stones that roll.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rolling Stones are the famous rock band, and marbles are literally small round stones that roll.

clue.text: Concerning wild oats

indicators.note: something wild is unruly and out of control, so these letters run riot into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A reference to sowing wild oats.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions introduce a topic: regarding, about, with respect to.

clue.text: Tudor drink

blocks.note: first meaning: the nickname of Queen Mary I, who burned Protestants
second meaning: the vodka and tomato juice cocktail

explanation.surface: A Tudor-era beverage.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary I of England, a Tudor monarch, earned the gory nickname, which was later given to a vodka and tomato juice cocktail.

clue.text: Dogfish on film

blocks.note: the setter runs two clue words together: its front half is the definition and its back half the first piece of wordplay
the bass is a food and sport fish
Spielberg's film E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial

explanation.surface: Dogfish shown in a film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dogfish' reads as a single word for a small shark, but it splits into the definition and the first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The basset is a short-legged, long-eared hound breed used for tracking.

clue.text: Rolled gold ware of inferior quality

indicators.note: rolled means tumbled over, so the letters that follow are turned into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Rolled gold, a thin layer over base metal, makes cheap jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: Rolled gold is a real cheap plating, so the whole surface is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of a poor grade is substandard, cheap and second-rate.

clue.text: Priest, perhaps, making well-known person  fulminate

blocks.note: short for celebrity
to fulminate is to rage or harangue

explanation.surface: A priest who turns a famous visitor into a ranting wreck.
explanation.definitionFit: A celebrant is the officiating minister at a Mass or Eucharist; 'perhaps' because a non-priest can also officiate.

clue.text: River and seafood the French found atrocious

blocks.note: the Exe is a river in Devon
crab is a shellfish eaten as seafood
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A restaurant critic finds the river fish and seafood dreadful.
explanation.definitionFit: Execrable means so bad as to be detestable; it is a strong word for dreadful or appalling.

clue.text: Insulting language from American imprisoned by Lincoln

indicators.note: a prisoner is shut inside a jail, so one word is locked within the other

blocks.note: Abe is Abraham Lincoln's familiar name
short for the United States

explanation.surface: An American locked up by Lincoln hurls insults.
explanation.definitionFit: Verbal abuse is offensive, insulting speech such as swearing or name-calling.

clue.text: Coal remaining at the end of three months

definitions.text: at the end of three months

blocks.note: first meaning: a glowing fragment left in a dying fire

blocks.clueFragment: at the end of three months
blocks.note: second meaning: the letters closing September, November and December

explanation.surface: Coal left burning at the end of a quarter.
explanation.definitionFit: A smouldering piece of coal left in the grate is a cinder of this kind, and Sept-, Nov- and Dec- all end in the same five letters.

clue.text: Scottish promontory with a German plant

blocks.note: a mull is a headland in Scotland, as in the Mull of Kintyre
ein is German for a

explanation.surface: A Scottish headland where a German plants something.
explanation.definitionFit: Mullein is a tall woolly-leaved wild plant of the figwort family, with spikes of yellow flowers.

clue.text: Almost 50% treasure birds

indicators.note: fifty per cent is a half, so only half of the word's letters are kept

blocks.note: the second half of the six-letter word
treasure means wealth

explanation.surface: Nearly half the treasure goes on birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost 50%' reads as nearly half, but 'Almost' is the word whose back half is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostriches are large flightless African birds, so they are examples of the defining class.

clue.text: Biscuit loaded with leaves?

blocks.note: loaded is slang for wealthy
tea is made from dried leaves

explanation.surface: A biscuit stuffed with leaves, perhaps a herbal one.
explanation.walkthrough: A Rich Tea is a plain, sweet British biscuit, traditionally dunked in tea, so the surface is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Rich Tea is a popular brand-style variety of plain sweet British biscuit eaten with a cuppa.

clue.text: We blame knitter for small woolly jumper

indicators.note: a knitter works yarn into a new pattern, so the letters are woven into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Blaming the knitter for an undersized woolly jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is British for a sweater, which fits the knitting surface; here it is a young animal that jumps about.
explanation.definitionFit: A young female sheep is little, covered in fleece, and frisks about leaping, so it is a woolly creature that jumps.

clue.text: Yseult's other name is Old English

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
standard abbreviation for English; the answer also runs unbroken through these words, a neat coincidence of the charade

explanation.surface: A note that the heroine's alternative name derives from Old English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old English' looks like a single language term, but only English is abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arthurian heroine loved by Tristan is spelt Yseult, Iseult or, in Wagner's opera, Isolde.

clue.text: Scale for winds in the open air

indicators.note: winds as a verb means twists or coils, so the letters are twisted out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wind-strength scale, like Beaufort's, for use outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winds' looks like a noun about weather; it is a verb meaning twists.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian loan phrase describes dining or painting outdoors, under the sky rather than indoors.

clue.text: Preserve the end of past prestige

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which is all that is kept

blocks.note: to cache is to store away safely
final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Keeping alive the last of former glory.
explanation.definitionFit: Cachet is distinction or standing that commands respect, a close synonym of status and kudos.

clue.text: Murderer outside second-class compartment

indicators.note: the killer stands outside, surrounding the class letter on both sides

blocks.note: Cain killed his brother Abel in Genesis
B grade is second class

explanation.surface: A killer waiting outside a second-class railway compartment.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabin is a private room on a ship or aircraft section, a kind of enclosed space or berth.

clue.text: Saucy book planted before man of brass

indicators.note: planted means placed or set down, so the book is put in front of the saucy word

blocks.note: a herbal is a book describing plants and their uses
pert means cheeky or impudent

explanation.surface: A racy book set down in front of a brass-necked man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Planted' does double duty in spirit: the book is a botanical one, and it is placed before the cheeky word.
explanation.definitionFit: Herb Alpert, trumpeter, led the Tijuana Brass, so he is literally a leader of a brass band.

clue.text: Clothes worn back-to-front for game

indicators.note: a garment worn back-to-front faces the wrong way, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: garb means clothing

explanation.surface: Wearing your clothes back to front as part of a party game.
explanation.definitionFit: Brag is a traditional British card game related to poker, with betting on three-card hands.

clue.text: Odysseus's first demand - to hold you once like a Cyclops

indicators.note: the hero's first means only the opening letter of his name is used
to hold something is to grip it inside, so the archaic word goes within the demand

blocks.note: initial letter of the hero's name
a need is a requirement or demand
ye is the archaic plural of you

explanation.surface: Odysseus's first demand of the Cyclops, in old-fashioned speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion lands just before the last letter of the demand. The surface fits: Odysseus blinded the one-eyed Polyphemus.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyclopes in Greek myth have a single eye in the middle of the forehead.

clue.text: Cell material in heart of young Rudge

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle, so the material goes into the centre of the young one

blocks.note: a baby is a young child
ribonucleic acid, found in living cells

explanation.surface: A biology lesson about the cells of a young person called Rudge.
explanation.walkthrough: Ribonucleic acid is the classic three-letter cell material in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnaby Rudge is the title character of Dickens's novel, so the given name pairs with that surname.
